hints: Focus on solubility rules here, adding calcium hydroxide adds lots of Ca2+ and OH- ions, so ask which new combination can form an insoluble solid.
Remember that all nitrates and most chlorides are soluble, but carbonates are insoluble except with Group 1 metals and ammonium.
Link the added Ca2+ with the carbonate and hydrogencarbonate already in the chalky water to see which insoluble salt must drop out of solution.
walkthrough:
**Spot what is added and what is already there**

Think of this as lime softening to remove temporary hardness. You are adding $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ from $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ to water that already contains $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{HCO}_3^{-}$, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and $\text{NO}_3^{-}$.

**Apply solubility rules**

Salts containing $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and $\text{NO}_3^{-}$ are almost always soluble in water, so $\text{CaCl}_2$, $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$ will stay dissolved. Carbonates are insoluble unless combined with Group 1 or ammonium ions.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{Group 1 and } \text{NH}_4^+ \text{ carbonates = soluble, all other carbonates = insoluble}$$

**Write the precipitation reaction**

The extra $\text{OH}^{-}$ converts soluble hydrogencarbonate into carbonate, which then meets $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and precipitates:
$$\text{HCO}_3^{-} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3(s)$$
This white solid is chalk or limestone reforming, and it is filtered off to soften the water.

options.A: Incorrect. Calcium chloride is very soluble in water because all common chlorides are soluble except $\text{AgCl}$, $\text{PbCl}_2$ and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$. No precipitate forms.
options.B: Correct. Calcium carbonate is insoluble, so $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ from the added lime combines with $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ (and $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ made from $\text{HCO}_3^{-}$ plus $\text{OH}^{-}$) to give solid $\text{CaCO}_3$ which precipitates.
options.C: Incorrect. All nitrates are soluble with no exceptions, so $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$ cannot precipitate. Students sometimes forget this universal rule.
options.D: Incorrect. All nitrates are soluble, so $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$ stays in solution. Magnesium can precipitate as $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ in lime treatment, but that compound is not listed here.
